cards.title: The world in seven pieces
cards.body: Earth's land is split into seven continents: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, and Australia. Asia is the biggest by far — it holds about 60 percent of all humans. Antarctica is the odd one out: a frozen continent with no permanent residents.

cards.title: Oceans glue it together
cards.body: Five oceans fill the gaps between continents: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Arctic. The Pacific alone covers more area than all the land on Earth combined. Every coastline you know touches one of these five.

Remember the seven with a silly sentence: All Ants Are Eating Apples Near Australia — Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Europe, Australia, North America... wait, that skips South America. Try: 'Aunt Annie Ate Eggs And Sausages' for Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Europe, Australia, North America, South America.

Find yourself on the map: pick any city you know, then name its continent, then the ocean nearest to it. Toronto? North America, Atlantic side. Sydney? Australia, Pacific side. Three facts per city, and the map starts feeling like home.

cards.explain: Asia dwarfs the rest — about 44 million square kilometers, roughly a third of Earth's land. Africa is second, North America third.

flashcards.back: Seven: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, Australia.
The Pacific — bigger than all of Earth's land put together.

flashcards.front: Which continent has no permanent residents?
flashcards.back: Antarctica. Only researchers stay there, and only temporarily.
Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Arctic.

questions.q: How many continents does Earth have?
questions.explain: Seven: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, Australia. Five is the number of oceans.

choices: Larger than all Earth's land combined
questions.explain: The Pacific covers about 165 million square kilometers — more than every continent added together.

questions.q: Which continent is the odd one out for population?
questions.explain: Antarctica has zero permanent residents. Australia has about 26 million people; Europe has over 700 million.
Toronto, Canada is firmly in North America. Its nearest ocean is the Atlantic.

questions.q: Which ocean touches Australia's east coast?
questions.explain: Australia's east coast — Sydney, Brisbane — faces the Pacific. The Indian Ocean is on the west.

cards.title: Three bands run the weather
cards.body: Earth has three main climate zones. The tropics wrap the equator — hot and wet all year. The temperate zones sit in the middle — that's where seasons happen. The polar zones cap the top and bottom — cold almost all the time. Your latitude decides your wardrobe.

cards.title: Rain has favorite addresses
cards.body: Tropical rainforests near the equator get rain nearly every afternoon. Deserts like the Sahara sit around 30 degrees north and south, where dry air sinks. Same planet, opposite weather — it's all about how air moves.
Latitude is the cheat code: 0° is the equator (hot), 23.5° marks the tropics' edge, 66.5° starts the polar circles. If you know a place's latitude, you can guess its climate before you ever visit.

Compare Quito, Ecuador (on the equator, but high in the Andes) with Singapore (on the equator, at sea level). Both tropical by latitude — but Quito feels like spring year-round while Singapore is hot and steamy. Altitude rewrites the rules latitude sets.

cards.q: Where do deserts like the Sahara mostly sit?
choices: Around 30° north and south of the equator
cards.explain: Dry air sinks around 30° latitude, squeezing out moisture. That's why the Sahara, the Arabian desert, and Australia's outback all sit near that line.

flashcards.front: What are Earth's three main climate zones?
flashcards.back: Tropical (hot, near equator), temperate (seasons, mid-latitudes), polar (cold, near the poles).

flashcards.front: Why is it hot at the equator?
flashcards.back: The sun's rays hit most directly there, year-round.
Around 30° north and south latitude, where dry air sinks.

flashcards.front: What can change a place's climate besides latitude?
flashcards.back: Altitude — high places are cooler. Quito sits on the equator but feels like spring because it's 2,850 meters up.

questions.q: Which zone gets all four seasons?
questions.explain: The temperate zones, between the tropics and the polar circles, tilt in and out of the sun — that's what makes spring, summer, autumn, winter.

choices: The sun hits most directly there
They're closest to the sun in space
questions.explain: It's about angle, not distance. Near the equator the sun's rays strike nearly straight down all year.
Global air circulation sinks dry air around 30° north and south. Some deserts have other causes, but this is the big pattern.

questions.q: Two cities on the equator can feel very different if...?
choices: One is much higher in altitude
questions.explain: Altitude cools things fast — about 6.5°C per kilometer up. That's why Quito feels springlike while Singapore swelters.

questions.q: Polar zones are cold mainly because...?
choices: Sunlight arrives at a shallow angle
questions.explain: Near the poles the sun stays low, so its energy spreads thin over a wide area. The ice reflecting heat back just doubles down on the cold.

cards.title: Capitals aren't always the biggest
cards.body: A capital is where the government sits — not necessarily the biggest city. Washington D.C. runs the US, but New York is far larger. Canberra runs Australia while Sydney gets the fame. Size and power live in different zip codes.

cards.title: Some capitals moved on purpose
cards.body: Brasília was built from scratch in the 1960s to pull Brazil's capital inland from Rio. Ottawa was picked as a compromise between Toronto and Montreal. Capitals are political choices, not popularity contests.
Learn capitals in pairs with a hook: Paris–France (fashion), Tokyo–Japan (tech), Cairo–Egypt (pyramids), Ottawa–Canada (polite), Canberra–Australia (not Sydney! — that's the classic trap).
Quiz yourself the fun way: name a country, then blurt its capital before three seconds pass. France — Paris. Japan — Tokyo. Egypt — Cairo. Speed beats staring at lists.

cards.explain: Canberra — the planned capital. Sydney is the famous one, which is exactly why this question traps people.

questions.explain: Cairo — home to about 20 million people in its metro area. Alexandria is the famous port; Giza holds the pyramids but isn't the capital.
Sydney is Australia's biggest city but Canberra is the capital. Ottawa and Paris are both real capitals.

choices: To move Brazil's capital inland from Rio
questions.explain: Brazil built Brasília from nothing in the late 1950s and moved the capital there in 1960, to develop the interior.

questions.q: Washington D.C. vs New York — which is the capital?
questions.explain: D.C. holds the government; New York holds the population and the money. Capitals are about power, not size.
London. Edinburgh is Scotland's capital, Manchester is a major city — but the UK's seat of government is London.
